title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: UM picks Textile Road for $1.2B Los Alamos facility—what it means for bills and land use.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy—the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're diving into the University of Michigan's decision to lock in the Textile Road site in Pittsfield Township for a massive high-performance computing campus tied to Los Alamos.
Exactly, Graham. This one feels different because it's not just another server farm—it's a billion-dollar supercomputer project with serious power and water demands right here in Washtenaw County.
Let's start there, Emmy. The university chose Textile Road today for this $1.2 billion facility. What stands out to you about the location and the scale?

The location in Pittsfield Township puts it in a spot where land use changes could ripple out fast. Residents thirty miles away will notice through utility rates and traffic, and I'm curious how this fits into the broader pattern we've seen with data centers across the state.

It does build on a running story. Michigan has seen multiple townships and cities pause or block projects over the last year because of exactly these concerns—power draw, water use, and how they affect local grids and farmland.
Walk me through the power side, Graham. A project like this tied to Los Alamos—how much electricity are we talking about, and who pays for the upgrades?

The facility will pull heavy loads, similar to other high-performance computing sites. Utilities like Consumers Energy and DTE have already flagged that new transmission lines are needed statewide to handle surging demand from AI and research facilities.
And those lines are sparking backlash from farmers who worry about lost acreage and property values. How does that connect to this UM project specifically?

The Textile Road site will add to that pressure in Washtenaw County. Even if the supercomputer itself isn't a traditional hyperscale data center, the power and water needs are comparable, and the university's choice reshapes local planning.
What about water? These facilities often need massive cooling. Is that a big factor here, or is the bigger issue the land itself?
Both matter. The project will draw significant water in a county already balancing growth and resources. Pittsfield Township will see direct land-use changes, while the rate impacts spread further.
I'm thinking about the residents thirty miles out. How exactly do electric bills rise from a project like this?

When utilities build new lines or generation to meet the demand, those costs get spread across all ratepayers. We've seen that play out in other states where data-center growth drove up bills for everyone.
And traffic changes—does the university expect construction traffic or ongoing operations to affect nearby roads?
The site choice will bring both during build-out and then regular operations. Local officials will have to manage that alongside the tax revenue the project could generate.
Who are the key players here besides the university? Los Alamos is the partner, but who else has a say?
Pittsfield Township zoning and planning, plus the utilities that will supply the power. State regulators could also weigh in on any environmental or grid impacts.
How long has this site selection been in the works? Any prior public discussion we should know about?
The announcement came today, but the university has been evaluating locations for high-performance computing expansion. This feels like the culmination of that process.
What happens next on the ground? Construction timelines, more hearings, or immediate pushback?

Expect site work to begin once permits clear, with township meetings likely drawing crowds similar to what we've seen in Morley and Rochester Hills. The lawsuit in Oakland County shows developers are ready to fight blocks in court.
That Oakland lawsuit—does it set any precedent that could affect the UM project or other Washtenaw plans?
It puts land-use authority and tax revenue questions in front of a judge. If the developer wins, it could make it harder for municipalities to say no to large projects on power and water grounds.
Rochester Hills just extended its ban another year for the same reasons. How many places are now in some kind of pause mode?

At least a handful across the state—Rochester Hills, Lowell is still drafting rules, and Whitehall Township is working on its first ordinance. The pattern is clear: communities want time to study impacts before approving anything big.
Detroit capped new facilities at small scale and DTE told planners the grid can't handle hyperscale. Does that make Washtenaw County more attractive for projects like UM's?
It could. Places with stronger grids or willing utilities become targets, which is why the Consumers Energy transmission fights are heating up in rural areas.
Farmers in those areas are protesting the new lines. What are their main worries beyond lost land?
Health effects from electromagnetic fields and depressed property values are the big ones. The utility says the lines are required for the demand, but locals want more study.
Morley residents packed a room and halted talks. Is that the kind of turnout we might see in Pittsfield?
Very likely. One hundred seventy people showed up in Morley over power, noise, and water. A university-backed supercomputer could draw even more attention.
Mount Pleasant's contract still has that Wisconsin-rejected power plant clause. Could something similar appear in the UM deal?
It's possible if the project needs dedicated generation. Out-of-state regulatory fights have already shown how they can shape Michigan bills.
Lowell is still months away from new rules. Any risk that projects slip through before standards tighten?
That's the concern local officials have raised—proposals could move under current weaker rules until the new ordinance is ready.
Whitehall Township is drafting its first rules on size, noise, and power. How does that compare to what Pittsfield might face?
Similar process—rural townships trying to get ahead of impacts before a big project lands. The outcome in one place often influences neighbors.
Overall, Graham, how do you see this UM announcement changing the statewide conversation?
It raises the stakes. A research institution like Michigan adds legitimacy, but the power and water demands are the same as commercial facilities, so the pushback will likely follow the same script.
And the bigger issue behind it all is really about who decides where these facilities go and who bears the costs.
That's the core tension—local control versus the economic and research benefits, with ratepayers and farmers often caught in the middle.
Thanks for laying that out. Let's move to some quick hits from around the state.
A data-center developer sued an Oakland County municipality today after officials blocked or delayed its project. The case puts land use, taxes, and power demand before a judge.
Residents there will feel any outcome in their electric bills and property taxes. It's a direct test of how far local governments can push back.
Rochester Hills extended its temporary ban on new data centers another year while it studies power, water, and noise. The pause stays in place for now.
That keeps large projects on hold and gives the city time to decide if the ban becomes permanent policy.
Consumers Energy's new transmission lines tied to data-center demand are drawing farm protests across Michigan. Lost acreage and property values are the main concerns.
The utility says the upgrades are required for AI demand, but rural residents want more say before lines cut through their land.
In Morley, a packed crowd forced officials to postpone any discussion of a proposed data facility. Power, noise, and water worries dominated.
The delay gives residents more time to organize before the project advances.
Detroit adopted rules capping new data centers at small scale so they don't strain the local grid the way massive facilities have elsewhere.
That protects residents from heavy rate hikes and noise while still allowing limited tech growth.
DTE told planners the Detroit grid is too weak for hyperscale centers. Six small ones already operate, but bigger ones are on hold pending studies.
Council members and residents are pushing for a moratorium until the impacts are clearer.
Yesterday in Mount Pleasant, the data center contract still includes a power plant provision already rejected in Wisconsin. Higher local energy costs remain a risk.
It shows how out-of-state regulatory fights can directly affect Michigan power bills.
Lowell officials said yesterday that new zoning and permitting standards for data centers won't be ready for several more months.
Until then, proposals could move under current rules, leaving residents with little say on power and water demands.
Whitehall Township reviewed its first draft ordinance yesterday, setting limits on size, noise, and power use in a rural area.
Muskegon County residents will see how those rules shape taxes and grid strain depending on what passes.
Now to what's on deck. Two meetings tonight that listeners can actually attend.
Lowell Township Planning Commission meets tonight on data center ordinance development and power concerns for the proposed Microsoft project.
And Portage City Council discusses the Data Center Industrial District zoning.
Both are live and open to the public—good places to hear directly from officials and neighbors.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: UM Supercomputer Campus Locked In as Power and Water Fights Spread
